title: Twelve months close
hookLine: two poets, twelve months each, one longing

lines: NANAK LOOKS BACK OVER THE YEAR.
A SECOND YEAR, BY GURU ARJAN.
cards: Two and ten. That's how the last stanza of Guru Nanak's poem counts the months: not twelve, but be das, two and ten, the way someone might count on their fingers at the end of a long year.
Once the Beloved has come home, the poem looks back over all of it. And the Guru Granth Sahib holds a second year like it, by Guru Arjan, in Raga Majh. Two poets, twelve months each.

teach.h: TWO AND TEN MONTHS ARE GOOD.
teach.b: Here's the end of Nanak's year, not word for word. The two and ten months, the seasons, the dates, the days are good.
The hours, the moments, the instants are blessed, when the True One comes and the meeting happens with ease. Hold that beside the whole year. Spring was good, and she ached.
The hot months were good, and she burned. The rains were good, and she lay awake. Nothing about the weather was wrong.
What changed was the meeting, and once it came, every month looked different looking back, even the hard ones.
Now set Guru Arjan's year beside it, which this path read in year two.
His months are in Raga Majh, and they too move from Chet around to Phalgun, a bride separated and asking to be united. In his Chet, remembering the Lord brings joy.
In his Asarh, the heat burns the ones who don't keep the Lord near.

teach.h: SAME BONES: A YEAR OF LONGING.
teach.b: Two Gurus, two ragas, two voices, sharing the same bones: a calendar the farmer and the bride both know, a longing in every month, and an ending where time itself is blessed. That's what a Barah Maha does.
It doesn't wait for one perfect season. It takes the ordinary year, every page of it, and lets each month carry the same love. Not one season is left out.
That's today's line: every season longs.

how: Both Barah Mahas are sung in kirtan and read in the Guru Granth Sahib; in some gurdwaras Guru Arjan's stanza for the new month is read on Sangrand, the first day of the month.

o: the last day of the Punjabi year, kept as a feast
the year's end, where every month is blessed by the meeting
a list of the year's twelve holy days for fasting

games.q: two years of longing — tap the pairs.
p: every month and moment is good

s: Nanak's last stanza calls only the month of union good
it calls all the months, seasons, days and moments good once the True One comes.
both Barah Mahas in the Granth follow a bride separated and longing
Guru Nanak's in Tukhari and Guru Arjan's in Majh share that longing.
a Barah Maha waits for one perfect season
it walks the whole ordinary year and lets every month carry the same love.

games.q: the Beloved has come home, and the bride looks back over the whole year, the aching spring, the burning summer, the sleepless rains. what does she say about those months?
o: they were all good, every month and moment.
games.why: the two and ten months, the seasons and days are good; the hours and moments are blessed when the True One comes.

practice: Bring back one season of your life that felt like waiting, a hard winter, a time when someone was missing, and let a few details return: the light, the smell, where you lived.
Then bring back a season that felt like arriving, hold the two side by side, and notice the part of you that was longing all along. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath, with thanks for both.

wordCard.voice: Twelve months close. Guru Nanak's year ends by calling every month, day and moment good once the True One comes, and Guru Arjan's year in Majh shares the same longing. Today's word.

orig.note: be das mah: 'two and ten months', how Nanak's last stanza counts the year.

carryVoice: Your line: every season longs. Even the waiting months belong to the year. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Tukhari, Mahala 1, Barah Maha, closing stanza, Ang 1109–1110 (the two and ten months, seasons, dates and days are good; hours and moments blessed when the True One comes)
Guru Granth Sahib, Majh, Mahala 5, Barah Maha, Ang 133–136 (Chet: remembering brings joy; Asarh: the heat burns those without the Lord near)
